plan.title: The Secret Empire Behind Your Glasses
alt_titles: The Orphan Who Built a $70 Billion Eyewear Empire
Why Your Glasses Cost So Much: The Luxottica Story
plan.description:
Ray-Ban, Oakley, LensCrafters, Sunglass Hut and a vision insurer: many of the eyewear names you know lead back to one company. This is how an orphan from Milan built EssilorLuxottica, and why glasses cost what they cost.

segments.narration: Take off your glasses, or your sunglasses, and look at the name on the side.
segments.image: File:Ray-Ban Aviator Shooter RB3139-001 3N (G-15 lenses) Size 62 09 160 Lens base 6.jpg

segments.narration: Ray-Ban. Oakley. Persol. Maybe Prada, Chanel or Armani.
Now think about where you bought them. Maybe LensCrafters, or Sunglass Hut, or Pearle Vision. Maybe your vision insurance helped pay.
segments.image: File:LensCrafters San Rafael - August 2022 - Sarah Stierch.jpg

segments.narration: It feels like a choice between dozens of rival brands and stores. It isn't.
A huge share of that path, the frame, the lens, the store and even the insurance, leads back to one company.
It's called EssilorLuxottica. In 2024 it brought in twenty-six and a half billion euros.
And it was built by a man who grew up in an orphanage in Milan.
segments.broll_query: old city street black and white

segments.narration: This is the story of how he did it, how he crushed a rival that dared to say no, and why your glasses cost what they cost.
To understand it, we have to go back to 1935.
Leonardo Del Vecchio was born in Milan in May 1935, to a poor family from the south of Italy.
segments.image: File:Milano - Duomo di Milano - Guglie, composizione - 2026-09-08 20-59-21 001.jpg

segments.narration: His father, a street vendor who sold vegetables, died before he was born.
His mother already had four other children, and could not raise another. So Leonardo grew up in an orphanage.
As a teenager, he became an apprentice to a tool and die maker in Milan. He learned to shape metal with extreme precision.
And he noticed that the tiny metal parts inside a pair of glasses were exactly the kind of thing he was good at making.
In 1961, at twenty-six, he moved to Agordo, a small mountain town in the Dolomites.
With two partners, he opened a workshop called Luxottica. It had ten employees, and it didn't make glasses. It made parts for other companies' glasses.
That's the detail that explains everything that came later.
Most people in his position would have been happy to be a reliable supplier. Del Vecchio saw it differently. Being a supplier meant someone else decided how much you were worth.
Del Vecchio hated depending on other people. If someone else made a part, someone else could raise the price or let you down.
So in 1967 he started making complete frames himself. By 1971, he stopped selling parts to anyone else.
From then on, every component of every frame was made inside his own company.
Hinges, screws, fronts, temples. While rivals bought parts from dozens of small suppliers, Luxottica answered only to itself.
That meant he controlled quality, cost and speed. If a design sold well, he could make more of it, faster, without asking anyone.
Then he went after the next link in the chain. In 1974 he bought Scarrone, the company that distributed his frames.
In 1981 he opened his first foreign subsidiary, in Germany. In 1988 he signed his first designer deal, with Giorgio Armani.
That deal was a turning point. A plain frame is a commodity. A frame with a fashion name on it can sell for many times the price.
In 1990, Luxottica listed on the New York Stock Exchange and raised eighty million dollars.
The same year, he bought Vogue Eyewear. The brand machine had started.
And the business worked. In 1994, Luxottica recorded a profit margin of fifteen point four percent, a record for the company at the time.
And now he had the money to do something much bigger. Stop being a supplier to the stores, and own the stores.
In 1995, Luxottica launched a hostile takeover of U.S. Shoe. The shoes didn't matter. What mattered was the company it owned: LensCrafters.
The price was one point four billion dollars. And the effect showed up on the shelves.
Before the takeover, about five percent of the frames LensCrafters sold were made by Luxottica. By 2002 it was seventy percent.
The same year, he bought Persol. In 1999, he bought Ray-Ban from Bausch and Lomb for six hundred forty million dollars.
segments.image: File:Bausch & Lomb Place, World Headquarters Building, Rochester, New York.jpg

segments.narration: In 2001, Sunglass Hut, for four hundred sixty-two million. In 2003, OPSM in Australia. In 2004, Pearle Vision.
segments.image: File:VINTAGE Sunglass Hut Kiosk; Oxford Valley Mall.jpg

segments.narration: Each deal did the same thing. It took a place where Luxottica had to compete for shelf space, and turned it into a place where Luxottica owned the shelf.
By 2001, Luxottica's sales had reached two point eight billion dollars, up twenty-seven percent in a single year. Profit was two hundred ninety million.
And every new store it bought became a new customer for its own factories.
And the designer licences kept coming. Chanel, Prada, Burberry, Versace, Dolce and Gabbana, Michael Kors, Coach.
To shoppers, these looked like competing luxury brands. Behind the scenes, many came from the same factories.
Almost everyone played along. Except one company.
segments.image: File:Dark clouds over Towers of Channelside, Tampa, FL.jpg

segments.narration: Oakley was the rebel of eyewear. Big, loud, sporty glasses, worn by athletes, made by its own company in California.
And Luxottica was one of its biggest sellers, through Sunglass Hut.
According to accounts of the fight, Oakley disputed the prices Luxottica wanted to pay. Oakley pushed back.
Luxottica's answer was simple. It dropped Oakley from its stores.
Overnight, Oakley lost a huge part of where its glasses were sold. Its stock price fell.
Think about the position that put Oakley in. Its biggest customer was also the owner of competing brands, like Ray-Ban.
Every shelf in Sunglass Hut that didn't hold an Oakley could hold something Luxottica made itself.
And then, with Oakley weakened, Luxottica made a takeover offer.
In November 2007, Oakley became part of Luxottica, for two point one billion dollars.
The lesson for everyone else in the industry was hard to miss. If you control the store, you control the brand.
Oakley kept its name, its look and its California image. Most buyers never knew anything had changed.
By now, the company also owned a vision insurance business, EyeMed. By 2014 it was the second largest vision benefits company in the United States.
Think about what that means. The insurer could steer you to a store that the same company owned, to buy a frame that the same company made.
segments.image: File:US Navy 050425-N-8629M-218 Lt. Robert Senko, an optometrist assigned to the Military Sealift Command (MSC) hospital ship USNS Mercy (T-AH 19), performs an eye exam on an Indonesian woman.jpg

segments.narration: Which raises the question everyone eventually asks. Why are glasses so expensive?
In 2012, the TV program 60 Minutes asked exactly that, in a report called Sticker Shock, and looked hard at Luxottica's grip on the market.
Then, in 2019, an unlikely critic spoke up. E. Dean Butler, the man who founded LensCrafters, the chain Luxottica had taken over.
He told the Los Angeles Times that glasses carried markups of nearly one thousand percent. He called it a complete rip-off.
Luxottica has always said its prices reflect design, quality and service. But the numbers on how much of the market it held are hard to ignore.
The company said its frames made up about ten percent of sales worldwide, and around twenty percent in the United States.
In 2015, it was the largest optical retailer in America. But the biggest move was still to come.
By then, Luxottica's retail arm ran about nine thousand one hundred stores around the world.
In 2014, it even teamed up with Google to work on Google Glass, the company's first big attempt at a computer you wear on your face.
It was a sign of how Luxottica saw itself. Not as a frame maker, but as the gatekeeper of anything people put on their face.
Glasses have two parts. The frame, and the lens. Del Vecchio owned frames. A French company, Essilor, ruled lenses.
In 2017, Essilor held about forty-one percent of the prescription lens market.
Market research firm Euromonitor put Luxottica's global share at fourteen percent, and Essilor's at thirteen. Their nearest rival, Johnson and Johnson, had under four.
That same year, the two companies announced they would merge. Regulators in Europe approved it in March 2018, without conditions.
On October first, 2018, EssilorLuxottica was born. Worth about seventy billion dollars on day one.
segments.image: File:Palazzo Mezzanotte - Piazza Affari - Milano - Italy.JPG

segments.narration: Together, the combined company held nearly thirty percent of the global eyewear market.
By 2019, it employed eighty-nine thousand people.
Frames, lenses, stores, insurance, designer licences. Almost every step between your eyes and your wallet.
Leonardo Del Vecchio, the boy from the orphanage, died in June 2022, at eighty-seven.
He was worth about twenty-four billion dollars, the second richest person in Italy.
But the machine he built kept running.
In 2024, EssilorLuxottica's revenue grew to twenty-six and a half billion euros, with an adjusted profit of three point one billion.
And it's already moving into the next thing your face might wear. Smart glasses.
segments.image: File:Brickell Ray Ban Meta Wayfarer Smart Glasses - Colorful facade.jpg

segments.narration: Its Ray-Ban smart glasses, built with Meta, had sold more than two million pairs by early 2025.
segments.image: File:Brickell Ray Ban Meta Wayfarer Smart Glasses - 2 May 2026.jpg

segments.narration: A few months later, Meta took a stake in EssilorLuxottica, reported at around three billion euros.
segments.image: File:Meta Platforms Headquarters Menlo Park California.jpg

segments.narration: So even if the future of computing ends up on your face, there's a good chance the frame will come from the same company.
Look at what that deal really is. One of the biggest tech companies in the world seemingly decided it was easier to buy into this empire than to compete with it.
Because to sell glasses at scale, you need the brands, the factories, the lenses and the stores. And one company already has all four.
segments.image: File:Selection of stylish eyeglasses displayed in organized trays for customers in an optical store during daylight hours.jpg

segments.narration: That's the real story of your glasses. Not a crowded market of rival brands, but an empire built one step at a time, by a man who never wanted to depend on anyone.
He started by making the smallest parts. He ended up owning almost the whole chain.
Whether that's brilliant business or a market with too little choice probably depends on which side of the counter you're standing on.
But the next time a pair of glasses costs more than you expected, you'll know exactly who to thank.
If you want more stories like this, about the companies hiding behind the brands you use every day, subscribe. Thanks for watching.
